claims.text: A dual-phase, graded-interface PVD coating will form an in situ adaptive tribofilm during sliding.
The coating will maintain low friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has an FCC microstructure.
The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has moderate tribological performance.
A coating approximately 1 µm thick containing an inert oxide such as Cr2O3 and a reactive phosphate-forming phase can be produced by an optimized PVD process.
A graded coating–substrate interface will enhance high-temperature adhesion and mitigate thermal-expansion mismatch.
Loads of 1–9 N and relative humidity of 25–40% are relevant controlled sliding-test conditions.
The proposed conditions replicate industrial contact pressures and thermal cycles.
Tribological stress will drive controlled coating reactions that create a continuous, self-replenishing lubricious tribofilm.
The graded interface will preserve coating integrity and adhesion throughout the proposed temperature range.
At lower temperatures, a lubricious glassy phase will reduce direct metal-to-metal contact.
At elevated temperatures, oxidation will produce a stable oxide network that improves high-temperature tribological behavior.
The high-temperature oxide network will integrate with a glassy phosphate binder to form an adaptive tribofilm.
The adaptive film will accommodate thermal expansion and reduce both adhesive and oxidative wear.
The coating will reduce coefficient of friction by at least 30% relative to uncoated CoCrFeNi across the entire room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The coating will significantly reduce wear rate relative to uncoated CoCrFeNi across the entire temperature range.
Tribofilm chemistry will undergo a noticeable transition near 700 °C.
Uncoated CoCrFeNi suffers higher-temperature performance degradation because of uncontrolled oxidation and lack of adaptive lubrication.
Performance may diminish under severe thermal shock, loads above 9 N, or environments markedly different from ambient air at 25–40% humidity.

contradictions.description: The oxide phase is described as inert in the intervention, but the mechanism requires selective oxidation of that same inert phase. It is unclear what additional oxidation or chemical transformation an already inert oxide such as Cr2O3 is expected to undergo.
